overview:
Sometime around the middle of the twenty-sixth century BCE, the Egyptian king Khufu, second ruler of the Fourth Dynasty, had a tomb raised on the limestone plateau at Giza, on the west bank of the Nile opposite what is now Cairo. It was built from roughly 2.3 million blocks, rising to about 146.6 metres on a base some 230 metres square, aligned to true north within a few minutes of arc. Stripped of its white Tura limestone casing by medieval builders quarrying for Cairo, it stands today about eight metres shorter, its stepped core exposed. For more than 3,700 years nothing taller was built anywhere on earth. The date usually given, around 2560 BCE, comes from reconstructions of the Egyptian king lists rather than from any inscription on the monument; radiocarbon samples from mortar in the masonry scatter across a range of some four centuries, and Old Kingdom dates in general run a century or two older than the historical chronology — an effect archaeologists attribute largely to builders burning long-dead timber. The precise year is a scholarly estimate, not a fact the Egyptians recorded.

Two discoveries in recent decades have transformed the picture of how the thing was actually made. From 1988, excavations at Heit el-Ghurab, a few hundred metres south of the Sphinx, uncovered more than seventeen acres of Fourth Dynasty settlement: bakeries, breweries, granaries, barracks, cattle bones, workshops and administrators' houses — the support town for the pyramid projects, demolished once the work was done. Then in 2013 a cache of papyri turned up at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast, the oldest inscribed papyrus known. Among them is the logbook of an inspector named Merer, who in the last years of Khufu's reign led a gang of some forty men ferrying casing limestone from the Tura quarries across the river to Giza, through a system of canals and basins engineered to bring boats close to the site. Merer's crew ate poultry, fish, dates and honey. Between them, the town and the diary confirm what Egyptologists had long argued: the pyramid was built by organised, provisioned, rotating work gangs in the king's service, not by enslaved multitudes.

The pyramid held three chambers — an unfinished one cut into bedrock, and two above it, the upper containing a granite sarcophagus, with roofing blocks of Aswan granite weighing up to eighty tonnes hauled some 900 kilometres downriver. Graffiti left by work gangs in the cramped relieving chambers above the burial chamber name Khufu, the closest thing to a builder's signature the monument carries. What remains genuinely open is the method: the configuration of ramps, the sequence of construction, how the near-perfect cardinal alignment was achieved. Muon-imaging surveys since 2015 have detected a large void above the Grand Gallery whose purpose nobody yet knows.
significance: It is the only one of the seven wonders of the ancient world still standing, and the reason the list was ever plausible: a building so far beyond the scale of anything around it that Greek and Roman visitors, already looking at something two thousand years old, could not account for it and reached for stories of tyranny and forced labour. That framing stuck for millennia and has only recently been dismantled by archaeology. Beyond its symbolism, the pyramid is evidence of something historically rarer than engineering skill — a state capable of quarrying, transporting, feeding, housing and accounting for tens of thousands of people across decades. The administrative machinery visible in Merer's ledgers and in the bakeries of Heit el-Ghurab is as much the achievement as the stone. It has also functioned, continuously, as a magnet for speculation, which is its own kind of significance: no other structure has attracted so much pseudo-archaeology, and defending the ordinary human explanation of it has shaped how Egyptology talks to the public.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica entries plus institutional archaeology pages on the Giza workers' town and the Wadi al-Jarf papyri; the dataset itself holds no events beneath this story, so nothing here is drawn from the map. Thin throughout: no Egyptian text describes the design or building of the pyramid, the 2559 BCE date is a modern chronological estimate that radiocarbon does not sharply confirm, the burial chamber was emptied in antiquity so nothing is known of Khufu's actual interment, and the construction method — ramps, lifting, alignment — is still argued over rather than settled.
